lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Polydeuces, you're heading up tomorrow, aren't you? If you see Menippus the Cynic anywhere — you'll find him in Corinth at the Craneum or in the Lyceum, laughing at the philosophers arguing with each other — tell him Diogenes says: if you've laughed enough at things up there, come down here. There's plenty more to laugh at. Up there your laughter was still uncertain — who knows what happens after life, after all? Here you won't stop laughing for real, like I'm doing now, especially when you see the rich and satraps and tyrants looking so humble and insignificant. You can only pick them out by their wailing, and they're soft and cowardly when they remember the world above. Tell him that. And tell him to fill his bag with plenty of lupines, and if he finds Hecate's supper lying at a crossroads or an egg from some purification or anything like that, bring it along.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: I'll report all that, Diogenes. But so I know exactly — what's he look like?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Old, bald, wearing a cloak patched so many times it's open to every wind and the rags are all different colors. He laughs all the time and mostly mocks those pretentious philosophers.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Shouldn't be hard to find from that.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Want me to give you a message for the philosophers too?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell them to stop their nonsense — arguing about the universe, growing horns on each other, making crocodiles, and teaching the mind to ask unanswerable questions.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: They'll just say I'm ignorant and uneducated for attacking their wisdom.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell them from me to go cry about it.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the rich, my dear Polydeuces, pass this on from us: Why do you fools hoard gold? Why punish yourselves calculating interest and piling talent on talent, when you'll be coming down here soon with just one obol?

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: That'll go to them as well.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the handsome and strong — Megillus of Corinth and Damoxenus the wrestler — tell them that down here the blond hair, the bright or dark eyes, the rosy cheeks, the strong muscles, the broad shoulders — none of it lasts. It's all just dust, they say. Bare skulls, no beauty left.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Easy enough to tell them that.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the poor, Spartan — there are plenty of them upset and pitying their own poverty — tell them not to weep or wail. Explain the equality here, and that they'll see the rich down here no better off than themselves. And if you like, give my regards to your Lacedaemonians and tell them they've been released.

lines.speaker: Polydeuces
lines.text: Nothing about the Lacedaemonians, Diogenes. I won't stand for it. But the rest I'll deliver.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Fine, we'll skip that. Just take the messages to the ones I mentioned.
